newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Hallenstein says cautious for rest of yr.
newsitem.headline: Hallenstein says cautious for rest of yr.

text.p: Retailer Hallenstein Glasson said on Friday it remained cautious for the rest of the 1997 financial year after reporting a half year net profit fall to NZ$4.8 million from $6.5 million.
The apparel retail segment in which the company operates was expected to remain difficult, Hallenstein said.

"The directors would like to emphasise that their future recommendations as to dividends will continue to be based on the trading performance and financial strength of the company and any growth opportunities it may be evaluating."
It said the summer season had seen some of the competition, especially in women's fashion, look to "rebrand" or exit the market segment.
There was also expected to be further penetration by Australian chains into the local apparel market over the next few years.
"However the company is financially strong, remains very committed to providing top quality customer service and ensuring its stores present a fresh and inviting environment for its customers."
Glassons early trading results from Highpoint Mall in Melbourne had been encouraging, and further stores in Melbourne were now being considered.
However, any further expansion into the Australian market was expected to be in a measured and orderly manner, Hallenstein said.
There was a focus for the winter 1997 season on rebuilding sales turnover for "like for like" stores, and trading margins, back nearer to that attained in winter 1996.
Longer term the company will continue aggressively to pursue increased market share.
Hallenstein said the summer season proved to be the most difficult faced by the company in recent years, with the New Zealand apparel market suffering from reduced consumer spending.

Hallenstein's market sectors were extremely competitive in the lead up to and immediately after Christmas, with the harsh trading conditions resulting in some of the company's competitors going into "sale" pre-Christmas, in an effort to boost sales and clear excessive stock holdings.
